analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the court, this is a federal estate tax case involving the marital deduction and is here on writ of certiorari to the Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit. Does a bequest of property in trust for the benefit of the surviving widow who is to receive a fixed-dollar monthly payment out of income in corpus and who is given a general power of appointment qualify for the marital deduction where an actuarial table is utilized to determine the value of the specific portion of the trust property within the meaning of Section 2056B, of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954. The will of the decedent bequeathed and devised one half of the residue in trust. The trustee was directed to pay the widow, out of income and corpus, the sum of $300 a month until the youngest child reached $18 and $350 a month thereafter for life. The widow was given a general power of appointment to appoint by will the principal remaining at the time of her death. Yes, Mr. Justice Harlan. Yes, Mr. Justice Harlan. The District Court decided that, notwithstanding the fact that the corpus was unable, up to the time of the hearing, to produce income of $300 a month, the marital deduction would not be available since income from the trust could have exceeded $300 a month and the surplus would then be required to be accumulated. Since the surviving spouse was not specifically entitled to all of the income of the trust corpus, the District Court reasoned that the marital deduction should not be allowed on that point. But then the District Court moved on to say, since they were assuming that the trust could generate more than $300 income, that they would apply an actuarial table to determine what the present value of the $300 a month would be and thus could carve out of the trust corpus that part which it would label a specific portion. The court of appeals for the marital deduction. The court of appeals for the marital deduction. The Court of appeals for the libertarians are invalid. itself casts doubt upon the regulation because it doesn't adopt it. It finds that it is unnecessary to determine the validity or invalidity. The Second Circuit in Geld, in 298 Federal Second, clearly takes the position that the regulations are invalid when insisting that the specific portion be a fractional or percentile of the trust. In that case, we had the widow entitled to the income, but there was a child who was entitled under the trust, if the trustee so determined, to up to $5,000 a year for education or maintenance. The Second Circuit took the position that the value of that $5,000, determined by actuarial tables, could be carved out of the trust corpus, and the balance, therefore, could be eligible for the marital deduction. The Seventh Circuit in Citizens National Bank of Evansville, 2 to 1, which is now number 488 in this court on a pending petition for writ of certiorari, likewise ruled that the regulations were invalid in a case very similar to the one at bar. When Congress put the marital deduction section on the books, it is stated in the hearings, and even in this court and staff, that equalization between common law citizens and community property citizens was designed. I would prefer to suggest that what Congress was aiming for was to cut down the discriminatory gap between the citizens of the states of the community property states and citizens of the common law states, because we cannot really have true equalization. Only in the classic case where the husband owns the family assets and dies first and following the rules of the road can we have this equalization. In various other situations, one Paul Anderson, writing in 54 Michigan Law Review, 1087, points out a number of postulates where there will be substantial inequality between the two property systems. There is no doubt that in a community property state the spouses own one half of the community property. However, we submit that Congress permits in a common law state a marital deduction if the wife is given a life estate and a power of appointment to her state or to others. We realize that if a widow only has a life estate with a remainder over to others, that such would not qualify for the marital reduction. We maintain that a widow who is entitled to receive $300 a month out of income and corpus and later $350 a month for her life and has the power to appoint to her state or to others, has the key incidents of ownership within the framework of this type of a statute. We don't have to prove that she has the equivalent of a fee simple because Congress recognizes that she wouldn't have a fee simple where she has a life estate with a power to appoint. We maintain that nowhere did Congress adopt a policy of value fluctuations on which the government lays the foundation of its regulations. The Second Circuit in Gelb finds no basis for such. But even if that were in Congress's mind at that time, we see that the at that time we say in the case at bar, if the value of the corpus increases, it will be includable in the gross estate of this widow when she passes away. Now, actuarial tables have been used on many occasions in determining valuation. The government stresses that in this particular case, had we used a capitalization approach, we would have had a value in excess of the trust corpus. And we take the position that, so long as the carving out process takes the lesser, whether it be the capitalization method or the annuity method, that that is the amount which should be allowed for the marital deduction, and not the hypothetical excess case. But we also feel that maybe it proves too much from the government's point of view. And that is, if it will take more money to give this widow $300 a month out of income and corpus, then it should follow that she is getting all of the income from the corpus. And that is, if it will be taxable, that it will be taxable in her estate. Consequently, we take the position that if the $300 is computed, the present value is computed on an actuarial basis, that the correct amount will be carved out of the trust corpus. The Third Circuit errant, we respectfully submit, in reading the will of this decedent in such a manner as to destroy the marital deduction. And we respectfully submit that the government's brief does not even attempt to support the reasoning of the Third Circuit majority opinion. For example, the Third Circuit majority opinion took the position that there would be a fund dissolution if we use the annuity basis of actuarial tables of carving out, and then says that the testator could not have contemplated. We stress in our brief that the testator said, out of income and corpus, and then went on to say, the principal remaining at the time of death, which indicates to us that the testator could have contemplated dipping into the corpus, number one, but also a dissipation. Nextly, the Third Circuit opinion stresses the spent thrift trust clauses in the will. And even the regulations of the commissioner of the treasury clearly provide that such spent thrift trust clauses will not inhibit the marital deduction. And nextly, there was stress made upon the time of death as being the wrong time to determine the valuation. And we know that that is the only time that we have to determine the valuation for marital deduction purposes in order to carve out the thing. What if the state here consisted of a 40-year 5% bond, that's all? 40-year 5% bonds, I believe the government would... With a direction to hold the bonds. With a direction to hold the bonds. No power to sell the bonds. The trustees had no power to sell the bonds. And the widow was entitled to all the income? No. Only the $300. $300 a month. In other words... All right. How much was it in money, Mr. Justice White? I mean, yes. What was it in money? Twice as much as was necessary to pay $300. Then we would take the position that you could only carve out that amount which would... But you would permit that. What's that, sir? You would say that marital deduction would be sustainable. We would say it would be sustainable so long she had that power to appoint upon her death. If she has the power to appoint upon her death the principle in that trust, that the marital deduction flows. Do you think, then, there's no necessity in the trust instrument to assign any specific portion of the corpus to her? Just, I mean, like, say, the income from half of the corpus. See, if... All of... In that situation, all that would be needed is to say $300 a month. Is she the sole beneficiary of this trust during her life? The sole beneficiary... She has the sole power to appoint by her... Upon her death? Let's just assume that the other... That the will says... The remainder of the income, if any, which there would be in my example, is paid to some other people. But she has the power to appoint these entire corpus. Then we would take the position that we would annual... We would take an actuarial table and determine the value of what she is going to receive income-wise and carve that out. And the reason I take that position is because you have now... How about the marital deduction? I would permit the marital deduction as to that part, which could be carved out, as determined by an actuarial table, for the reason that you have now indicated that she does not have all of the income of the specific portion, but she does have the authority to give away all of the trust corpus by her will to her state or to others. Consequently, we satisfy the latter part, but we don't satisfy the magic words, all of the income. And because we know that she is going to get half of the income, then I believe that even the government would admit that we would be allowed a marital deduction as to that one half. Certainly, Mr. Justice White's question puts an easier case for you than your case, doesn't it? Yes. Oh, yes. Even the government's example in its brief produces that. Oh, yes. To me, it's an easier case than our case. Our case is $300 a month out of income and corpus is what we're stressing. Right. And basically, are we going to say that Congress would have balked at the use of an actuarial table in carving it out? This really comes down to the meaning of the statutory phrase, a specific portion thereof, doesn't it? You've put your finger on it exactly, Mr. Justice. I would like to make one more point and reserve the balance of my time, if I may, for rebuttal. The rules were proposed, the regulations were proposed, in October of 56. The will was written in January of 57. January of 57. The death occurred May 3, 58. The rules were promulgated June 23, 58. Therefore, those who were watching proposed rules would have known. Those who were waiting for final rules would not have known under the context of this case. Therefore, we respectfully submit that we should not be expected to have these regulations take the form of law because of being on the books quite a bit of time. I'd just like to reserve the balance of my time. Mr. Pugh. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the Court. This case turns on whether a decedent's bequest to his widow of fixed monthly payments from a variable yield of trust constituted a bequest of all the income from a specific portion of the trust, as Section 2056B5 requires, if that bequest is to qualify for the marital deduction. The key words we here submit are all of the income from the specific portion, which must be given to the widow if the bequest to her is to qualify for the marital deduction. The legislative history and the purpose of Section 2056B5 make it clear that Congress has required that the widow be given all the income from a specific portion of trust property in order to ensure that she'll have the rights of a virtual owner in that portion, in order to ensure that her income will rise and fall with the actual income generated by the trust property, just as an owner's would. The widow must receive the rights of a virtual owner because it follows from Congress's intent to achieve estate tax equality between common law and community property states that a bequest of trust income to a widow in a common law state should not be tax-exempt unless the widow receives rights equivalent to those enjoyed by a spouse in a community property state in her share of the community property. The petitioner here argues that since the value of the widow's right to receive fixed payments can be estimated through an annuity computation based on various arbitrary assumptions, that estimated value can be considered a qualifying specific portion under the statute. We submit that whether a bequest in trust qualifies under Section 2056B5 turns not on whether the widow's interest can be valued, but on whether the widow has been given the rights equivalent to virtual ownership that are specified in Section 2056B5, including the right to receive all of the income from a specific portion of the trust property during her lifetime. Furthermore, the basic objective, Your Honor, of the marital of this particular section, Section 2056B5, was to give the estate of marital deduction for a portion of trust property if the widow received in that portion of trust property the rights of virtual ownership. Yes, I understand, but I'm still asking you what. Well, it's necessary to do that. As I understand the theory of it, Congress wanted to equalize the advantages that were obtained by surviving widows in community property states. Now, why is it necessary, as a matter of policy, which is what you've been arguing here, as I understand it, apart from the specific wording of the statute, which you're also arguing, why is it necessary as a matter of policy to look through the technicalities and have them? I think you're right. This is set up perfectly obvious here that the husband intended the wife to get $300 a month out of the income of the estate with power and invade principal. Now, is there any reason of congressional policy why that should not be honored? Sure, and I think it stems basically from the congressional purpose to equalize the estate tax effects in community property in common law states. Congress wanted to ensure that a bequest of trust income to a widow in a common law state should not qualify for the marital deduction unless the widow received rights that were equivalent to the outright ownership enjoyed by a spouse in a community property state in her share of the community property. There's no doubt that the widow here had a power appointment. Is that so? Yes, sir. She had a power appointment over the entire corpus. And the problem is whether, like an owner, she had a right to receive all of the income from an identifiable portion of trust property. I suppose, as a matter of fact, in order to produce, in order to pay her $300 a month, $3,600 a year, there does have to be an invasion of corpus. She gets all the income plus, doesn't she, as a factual matter of the real world and how much you can hire out money for. Well, no, Your Honor, with respect, the court below held that while the trust had not generated enough income to produce the $300 per month payments. The corpus was capable of producing that much income. The corpus was about $70,000, a little less, wasn't it? And the court specifically held... And in order to produce $3,600 a year, that's 5-plus percent interest. Yes, 5.5 percent interest on the initial value of the corpus would have produced enough to make these payments to the widow. The court below held that for that reason, because the corpus was capable of producing more than the income required to produce the $300 per month payments, the widow was not receiving all of the income from the entire corpus. It's quite possible that one could be accumulated. How do they made that finding, that this corpus was capable of producing more than that? There's nothing in the record, Your Honor, that indicates what the precise yield of the corpus was. And I take it the court reached this finding on the basis of its own deduction, that a corpus of $70,000 could be capable of producing more than $3,600, if not now, then at some point in the future. Plus there could be an increase in the capital value. Yes, the statute clearly requires that the widow be entitled to receive all of the income from the entire trust corpus throughout her lifetime. And in a period of rising values, it's entirely possible that a trust corpus of this magnitude would produce more than enough income to enable payment of the $300 per month, at which point the excess income would be accumulated. Well, if it turned out that the corpus, total corpus of the trust was $5,000 in order to pay $300 a month, would you make the same argument? I think, Your Honor, in a case as clear as that, it would be, I think, quite obvious that the widow would be entitled to receive all of the income from the entire corpus, and therefore the entire value would qualify. What about my example, your opponent on the bond? Well, Your Honor, the regulations in requiring that a specific portion be cast in terms of a fractional share or its equivalent don't require that the magic language of fractional share or percentile interest be used. I think in your example in which you've got a fixed yield trust from which the widow is to receive in the form of fixed payments, half the income generated by the trust, we would clearly have a bequest to the widow that would be the equivalent to a fractional share, namely one half. You just say here that on the peculiar facts of this case, there just isn't any limitation that is the equivalent of a fixed share. Your Honor, we submit that at the decedent's death, we have to be able to point to a specific portion of the trust property from which the widow will receive all of the income that's actually generated through her lifetime. The petitioner suggests that we can use an annuity valuation to isolate a specific portion. But we submit that since the annuity computation is based on the assumption that the corpus will have a fixed constant yield of three and a half percent, whereas in fact, the yield from this trust corpus is going to vary, that computation cannot serve to isolate a specific portion of this trust corpus from which the widow will necessarily receive all of the income throughout her lifetime as an owner would, and as we submit, the statute clearly requires. It is a common, excuse me, go ahead. It's a common place in tax law generally to use this kind of computations, isn't it, in figuring out the value of remainders and so on? Yes, Your Honor, and certainly the use of this kind of computation to figure out the value of an interest such as a remainder or annuity that has to be included in the gross estate is entirely appropriate and extremely helpful. We submit, however, that this kind of a computation, based on an assumed fixed yield of 3.5% is entirely inappropriate when the question is whether the widow was given the rights of virtual ownership prescribed in Section 2056B5. It's inappropriate because the annuity assumes a fixed constant yield of 3.5%, whereas, in fact, no one knows what the yield of this trust will be over the future. What would that amount to here? What would the use of the annuity table amount to? Well, Your Honor, actually two techniques of valuation of the widow's rights have been used by the lower courts. The court in this case used an annuity computation which resulted in a $63,000 specific portion. The Seventh Circuit Court of Appeals has approved a capitalization approach. Under the annuity approach used by the court below, a computation is made of the amount of corpus that would be required to pay an annuity of $300 per month over the theoretical life expectancy of the widow using both the corpus and the income at an assumed fixed yield of 3.5% on the assumption that the corpus would be exhausted at the end of the theoretical life expectancy of the widow. The capitalization approach that's been used by the district court in the Citizens National Bank which is pending on the government's petition for certiorari here and which was approved by the Seventh Circuit! involves simply a computation of the amount of the corpus which at a fixed yield of 3.5% would throw off $300 per month assuming no exhaustion or diminution of the corpus. And that would be like, what would that work out to do here? In this case, that would be a capitalization approach would result in a valuation of $103,000 for the widow's right to receive fixed payments. Of course, this is vastly in excess of the full value of the trust corpus, $69,000. The corpus in this case had been $20,000. Would you have the same case? Well, I think that in a period of rising values it's difficult to predict what the future yield of a particular piece of property will be. and in a very short time that $20,000 would be greatly reduced. Well, I think that your honor, if it were clear that the trust corpus would not generate enough income to produce the fixed monthly payments, then it would be proper to conclude that the widow was receiving all of the income from the entire trust corpus. Therefore, the entire trust corpus would qualify for the marital deduction. You mean, I think you mean not only that she was, but that she would have to be under any kind of condition. I think it would be necessary to show clearly that the widow would necessarily be in excess of the actual income generated by the trust property. If you had a $20,000 trust here, and on that reasoning, does that mean that that would qualify? I think we'd have to show, your honor, that it really was clear that the trust could never produce enough income to meet the $300 per month payments to the widow. And I think if the court concluded that it was clear the trust could not produce enough income to meet those payments, then it would be proper to conclude that the widow was receiving all of the income from the entire trust. That involves a judgment as life expectancy too. Well, we submit, your honor, that the method of computation used by the court below here is entirely inappropriate not only because it's based on an assumed fixed yield of 3.5%, whereas no one knows what this corpus is going to yield over the entire remaining lifetime of the widow, but also because it introduces into the computation the widow's life expectancy so that the value of the widow's right to receive fixed payments and therefore the size of the specific portion under petitioner's contention depends upon the age of the widow at the death of her husband. The younger the widow, the larger the marital deduction. We submit there's no support in the statute or in the legislative history to justify this result. In the trust estate here, the corpus were $20,000 and you say that Maddie van der Meritone production would be available. In that situation, you're also making some assumptions as to the widow's life expectancy. Well, I think, Your Honor, with respect that it would be necessary to show that the $20,000 corpus could never, could clearly not produce enough income to meet the monthly payments to the widow in order to conclude that the widow was entitled to all of the income from the corpus throughout her lifetime. If the nature of the property were such that its income might rise dramatically, then we would submit that it would be improper to conclude in that case that the widow would be entitled to all of the income from the trust corpus. Don't you value things at the time of death? Yes, Your Honor, it's clear that if we were talking about the value of a remainder or indeed the value of an annuity that had to be included in gross estate, we'd go to these tables to do so. But we submit it's inappropriate to use these tables for the purpose of determining whether the widow has been given the rights of virtual ownership in a portion of trust property that are prescribed in section 2056B5. It's inappropriate to use a computation that's based on a fixed hypothetical 3.5% yield. I know you say that, but that's the way tax values are said, aren't they? At the time of death or one year after? We submit basically, Your Honor, this is not a question of valuation. The question under 2056B5 is whether the widow received the rights equivalent to virtual ownership in an identifiable portion of trust property. Could the widow have taken against the will here? I'm not an expert on Pennsylvania state tax law, but I would assume so, Your Honor. And what would have been the situation then? If the widow takes against the will and takes an absolute interest under state law, that's an interest passing from the decedent to the widow that would qualify for the marital deduction. She would have had half of the interest to pass from the decedent to her. But it's not unusual, I submit, Your Honor, for... I'm not making the argument, I just wanted to know. I think if the widow could take against the will, the interest, depending upon its characteristics under state law, could qualify for the marital deduction. What would that have been here? If she had gotten half? The full value of the trust was $69,000, and if under state law she would be taking half of that, it would be... What was allowed in here? Beg your pardon? And what was the claim here of the petitioner for the marital deduction? How much? The petitioner originally claimed the full value of the trust corpus as qualifying for the marital deduction, and then, relying on the annuity computation, claimed a lower amount which resulted from that computation of $63,000. We submit, Your Honor, that it is inappropriate to use an annuity computation of this kind because it's based on the fixed 3.5% yield. When the statute says the widow has to receive all the income from a specific portion of the trust property, it surely means all the income that may ultimately be generated during the widow's lifetime, and not merely a fixed hypothetical yield of 3.5%. To make a firm, Mr. Pugh, but suppose the court below, on the basis of evidence, had found a $70,000 stake that did not produce enough income to pay this woman $300 for the rest of her life. Huh? Now, why wouldn't she be entitled to the marital deduction then? Basically, Your Honor, because we can't point to a specific portion of the trust property. This is a whole trust, isn't it? $70,000? Just, why is this exactly like the $20,000 illustration? Because it's extremely difficult. Well, the point, the question is whether the widow will necessarily receive all of the income actually generated by this portion of the trust throughout her lifetime. I'm suggesting that to you. Suppose that the court finds that, on the basis of evidence, that $70,000 can't possibly throw off enough income to pay the $300 a month, and therefore the woman will get all of the income from all of the estate. Why doesn't that qualify? Under those circumstances, Mr. Justice Portis, I think the request would qualify because the widow would be receiving all of the income from all of the trust corpus during her lifetime. $70,000, I'd say, throw off $300 a month, you'd have to start hitting the jackpot right away, wouldn't you? Well, I think it's very difficult. We're talking about the widow's life expectancy here. She was 42 at the death of the decedent. She might well have a life expectancy of another 25 years, and I think it's difficult to say that a particular trust corpus, suppose it were Blackacre, could not increase in yield over that life expectancy. Yeah, but it might increase or might decrease or might go sideways. Yes, and I think that illustrates the necessity to utilize a fractional share approach in interpreting a specific portion, because in order to ensure that the widow will receive the rights of a virtual owner in any portion of trust property that qualifies for the marital deduction, that portion we submit has to be cast in terms of a fractional share or its equivalent, because only in that way can we isolate, at the time of the decedent's death, as we must, a specific portion of the trust property from which the widow will necessarily receive all of the income throughout her lifetime. If we take a bequest such as Blackacre, if the widow is given all of the income from one half of Blackacre, plus the general power of appointment over that one half, it's clear that her interest, this bequest will qualify. Blackacre was given away when I was in law school. What is this? Is it security is what? Well, I'm assuming in this case we have Blackacre, which is a piece of real property. I take it the corpus of the trust that we're dealing with here consists of something other than Blackacre, although the record is not so indicated. But if the widow is given the $4,000 from the yield of Blackacre, whatever it may be, and in the first year that yield is $8,000, at that point the widow is receiving all of the income from one half. But if at some point in the future, Blackacre's yield rises to $16,000, then the widow is receiving all of the income from only one quarter. And if the yield from Blackacre continues to rise over the life of the widow, eventually the widow may be receiving all of the income from only a very small portion, indeed, of the property concerned. Therefore, we submit only by requiring, as the regulations do, that the widow's income interest be cast in terms of a fractional or percentile interest or its equivalent, will it be possible at the decedent's death to isolate a specific portion of the trust property from which the widow will receive all of the income necessarily throughout her lifetime, just as an owner would and as the clear language of Section 2056B5 requires. And I think that this result really is dictated clearly by the legislative history of Section 2056B5. Congress initially enacted the marital deduction provisions in 1948 to equalize the estate tax effects in community property and common law jurisdictions. The widow in the community property state is the outright owner of her one half of the community property. Therefore, Congress felt that it was essential to ensure that any property transferred to a widow in a common law state convey to the widow the rights of virtual ownership if that request was to qualify for the marital deduction. Congress recognized that the requests in trust are used very often in common law states, so Congress provided that if the widow is given under a trust instrument all of the income from the trust corpus during her lifetime and the general power of appointment over the entire corpus, the request would qualify because the widow had two key characteristics of virtual ownership. Her income would necessarily rise and fall with the income generated by the trust property during her lifetime and the value of the property subject to her power of appointment would rise and fall with changes in value of the underlying trust assets. And this principle was applied in 1954 in Section 2056 B.5 with respect to a bequest of less than all of the income from the trust corpus. But the widow did have to receive, clearly under the statutory language, all of the income from a specific portion of the trust property. When was this will drawn? The will was drawn in January of 1957, Your Honor. The regulations adopting the Treasury's interpretation of a specific portion were issued in 1956, October 16 of 1956, so that practitioners were aware of the service's interpretation as of that point. I think, Your Honor, the problem can be avoided very easily through drafts. And, I mean, the typical mechanism would be to give the widow all of the income from a specified portion of the trust corpus, but give the trustees the right to invade corpus if necessary to bring her payments up to a stated level. I would think that a provision of this kind would not be unusual. Not would not be unusual. I think it would not be uncommon for the testator to want to assure his surviving spouse of a stated amount of current income. Yes, there are a number of ways of doing it, the way I just described, and also you could say the widow shall receive $6,000 per year. I think it's clear that the practitioners who are aware of the service position on issues of this kind would not fall into this trap. The problem really didn't arise until the specific portion language was introduced into the marital deduction provision in 1954, and the service promulgated its regulations in 1956. This presumably would have been in time for most state planners to be aware of the service's position in time to make the necessary adjustments. I would think that our position would probably have to be the same, Your Honor, in view of Congress's purpose to ensure that no bequest in trust qualify for the marital deduction unless it gave to the surviving spouse an interest that was equivalent to the interest that a surviving spouse in a community property state enjoys in her share of community property. We really have to find an interest in the trust property with respect to which the surviving spouse has the kind of rights that a widow in a community property state has in her share of community property. Namely, she has to receive all of the income from that particular portion of trust property, whatever the future fluctuations of the income may be over her lifetime.
